plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: It separates hard outcomes from judgment. Attract mode, dev sliders, the 10-foot rules and music at 10% are exact, while genre, perspective and research are left to me. The This computer section was the most useful part: real browser versions and named stand-ins for what the machine lacks told me what could be proved here. Writing for builders who cannot ask me questions also pushed me to test the risky assumptions rather than guess at them.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Three things. First, 'Multiplayer: follow the hub for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own'. The protocol only covers sessions and says the game is not affected outside one, so I could not tell whether on its own meant simply still runs, or also needs multiplayer. I took it as: it runs normally, plus couch co-op on one screen, which the hub's own docs call the game's own, and the plan says so. Second, TASK.md says the browsers are already downloaded and not to install them, while the game AGENTS.md and the new-game output say to run scripts/setup.sh, which downloads Chrome and Node. Third, 'leave out TASK.md's file and folder names' did not say whether the exit interview file counts, so I left out every one and referred to them by role. A smaller one: the title may riff on the source's name, but it was unclear how far the source's subtitle can appear as a theme. I kept it to the ordinary phrase in dialogue.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: Making the plan true rather than plausible. The public API gives game code no way to reach the 3D scene or import three.js, and surgery needs tissue that deforms live, so I had to find a legal route and prove it: keep the geometry a defineGeometry builder returns and rewrite it each frame. Multiplayer was harder. Reading the protocol predicted none of the three failures the real harness showed: the engine refuses to start on the hub's ?aihub query keys, connect has to come before the engine boots because of the 10 s hello window, and ready has to come before the GPU warm-up because the harness waits only 20 s. After those fixes, a small host-sequenced lockstep prototype passed all four harness runs with matching hashes. Keeping all of this to a plan a builder can actually read was the other half of the difficulty. Checking coverage honestly was hard too. My first requirements table was only my own claim, and when I audited every TASK.md line against the plan, with that table excluded, it found 29 unmet items. Three were real design gaps: nothing showed players what they cannot do, there was no issue log to answer the Testing Feedback counts, and the catalogue suggestions were incomplete. Testing also showed my no-WebGPU message could never have appeared in Firefox.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: Fix or disclose the run environment first. TMPDIR is too long for a Unix socket: Chromium dies with 'Socket path too long' and tsx fails with EINVAL, and node x shot hung for over 4 minutes before I found it. The only fix I found is a short directory under /tmp, which goes against TASK.md's rule against /tmp, so either set a short TMPDIR for runs or allow that exception. Also give CHROMIUM_PATH and say not to run scripts/setup.sh, since the engine does not look in Playwright's browser folder by default. Reword the on-its-own multiplayer sentence so it says whether standalone multiplayer is required, and say whether the planner may prototype and how long the plan should be. For the owner rather than the prompt: the engine should ignore or warn on unknown query keys, offer a public way to draw a live mesh, and offer a one-file build for games instead of only the playground. Its guide also cites labs/playground, which a game does not get. Numbering TASK.md's requirements would also help: they are mixed in with machine facts over about 110 lines, so neither a planner nor a builder can easily prove nothing was missed.
